J’ai du changer de site pirate 5 fois pour regarder ce film normalement, l’avantage c’est que je comprends mieux pk je l’aime vrm pas Nolan. Déjà J’ai un gros problème avec les films qui misent tout sur l’immensité inaccessible au détriment des subtilités du quotidien et la transmission d’idées qui sont un tout petit peu plus complexes que “grosse planète stylée dans le vide”. D’un côté, c’est juste une question de goût (et de dégoût), mais d’un autre ce n’est pas pour rien que les blockbusters ont toujours la même geule et que c’est toujours les mêmes sociétés de productions derrière; faire un film sur l’espace comme le fait Nolan est rentable parce que tout le monde a envie de voir des trous noirs et des planètes en IMAX (i.e. : c’est facile à regarder). Après, chaque production à la Warner Bros et Paramount (dream team) réserve son lot de surprises, comme ici. En soit, les questions posées sur les idéaux humains de progrès et de constant dépassement VS l’immanence de la vie matérielle, tangible et ce qu’elle a d’indispensable AURAIENT PU être giga intéressantes si cette manie de colonisation et de survie de l’espèce humaine (en l’occurrence une consortium d’hommes blancs et virils) n’était pas présentée comme le ferait un enfant de 5 ans ou tout simplement Elon Musk, c’est à dire sans nuance ou avec si peu que c’en est irritant. “L’humain n’a jamais été destiné à rester sur terre” ou jsp quoi bullshit, ce récit n’est JAMAIS REMIS EN CAUSE comme étant un ego trip mais juste intergalactique; la conclusion du film est que Cooper se retrouve effectivement sur une station extra-terrestre que sa fille a réussi à installer et youpiii on a échappé à cette terre remplie de poussière donc happy end grâce à la NASA, merci les états-uniens vous êtes les boss de la Terre (je crois ne même pas exagérer les côté ultra patriotique du film). C’est terrifiant de se dire que dans la tête de Nolan la question de la survie de l’espèce humaine par la colonisation de l’espace constituait un projet de film sérieux, et c’est dire à quel point y’a r dans le crâne de ce gars, premier degré il m’a introduit à un nouveau type de fanatisme à ce niveau là, celui autour de la glorification de la race humaine qui a été capable de rendre une planète entière inhabitable pour elle et pour les autres formes de vie (dans le scénario de Nolan, bien sûr, c’est pas DU TOUT vrai et je ne trouve pas que c’est limite absolument frustrant de voir un mec de cet âge fantasmer sur des échappatoires fantaisistes à la fin du monde alors que la Terre est aujourd’hui EFFECTIVEMENT inhabitable à certains endroits et que cette destruction n’est pas contingente mais bien le résultat des décennies passées de libéralisme à l’américaine que l’autre semble si avide de défendre ici avec son discours à deux balles sur le progrès et les ingénieurs). En bref, j’ai jamais cru pouvoir vraiment m’énerver face à l’anthropocentrisme humain, mais Nolan a réussi ladies and gentlemen. Par la suite le film prouve de façon extrêmement douloureuse qu’il mise véritablement tout sur le visuel et l’immensité lorsqu’on se rend compte à quel pont le dialogue est atrocement stérile et limpide, comme avec les interactions entre Brand (vieux) et Murph qui sont tout droit sorti d’un rom com, avec Murph qui l’appelle “professor” à CHACUNE de ses putains de répliques et le dialogue à l’hôpital oh mon dieu je priais pour que ça s’arrête enfin. Idem pour la dynamique entre Murph et Tom adultes qui est tout bonnement incompréhensible, quelques-uns de mes moments préférés en termes de frustration engendrée : -La scène de repas chez les Cooper avec la famille du côté de Tom + Murph, scène qui dure genre 20 secondes et qui sert juste à montrer que Murph refuse de retourner dans sa chambre car trop triste (le dialogue est inexistant, je ne comprends pas l’utilité de ces 20 secondes) -La scène d’altercation entre Tom et le médecin, là c’était du haut niveau de bullshit j’ai adoré. Donc Tom s’énerve TELLEMENT en l’espace de 2 nanosecondes (il vient de rentrer quand il voit que Murph essaye d’éloigner les enfants de la maison car trop de poussière et que l’enfant tousse mais Tom attaché à maison car ne cope pas de la même manière que Murph donc ça lui déplaît) qu’il en vient tout de suite à juste bah frapper le médecin logique c’est pas juste qu’il y a un éléphant dans la pièce qui ne sait pas écrire de putains de dialogues pour exprimer l’état d’âmes des personnages -et mon PRÉFÉRÉ, mon chouchou d’amour c’est la scène où, Murph, après avoir brûlé le champ de la maison (?????????? D’ailleurs mais bon) puis être restée deux décennies dans la maison Cooper pour trouver des indices qu’aurait pu laisser son père qui gravite dans la dimension des étagères de livre, ressort de la maison avec la montre qu’elle a trouvée et accueille Tom (qui, on le rappelle, revient du champ qui brûle après l’avoir découvert donc PAS d’interaction entre les deux entre le moment où Murph va incendier le champ et le moment où elle est devant la maison et que Tom y retourne) donc accueille Tom en secouant la montre à gauche et à droite et en criant “Il (papa Cooper) nous a sauvés”. À ce stade Tom ne peut pas VOIR le message en morse que contient la montre et par extension ne peut pas comprendre ce que raconte Murph, mais, sans remettre en cause ce que lui dit sa sœur pyromane, il décide de juste…bah lui donner un gros câlin ouais un gros câlinou et on ne reparle plus jamais du champ brûlé. La décision de Murph de brûler le champ n’engendre aucun conflit entre les deux personnages et c’est absurde à quelle vitesse Tom change de personnalité et askip comprend tout de suite ce que veut lui dire Murph (peut être parce que qlq ne sait pas écrire un conflit s’il implique un peu plus de complexité que juste des gros plans sur des personnages qui pleurent pour montrer qu’ils ne sont vrm pas contents). En fait TOUTES les scènes qui se passent sur Terre et qui sont tellement hâtées ou mal écrites ou incroyablement courtes que ça ressemble à un montage vidéo de moments épars plutôt qu’à un ensemble construit et qui a du sens (de toute façon ça n’en a pas), toutes ces scènes nous montrent Interstellar sans les grosses planètes, donc le fond de ce film, à savoir un gros vide (le trou noir rencontré par papa Cooper à la fin du film serait donc une métaphore de l’écriture de Nolan ??😱😱😱). Et je parle de vide d’autant plus que, ce film qui veut explorer “l’humanité” à la fois par ses transports liés à la survie de l’espèce et à la survie de l’individu, est incapable de produire ne serait-ce qu’une seule scène qui évoquerait un moment humain, que ce soit par le langage, la relation entre deux personnages (à part papa Cooper et Murph aller on te l’accorde Nolan) ou juste les plans. Il a cru que ça suffisait de glisser deux trois vers d’un très bon poème tout au long du film pour y rajouter un côté profond et intellectuel, mais ça marche pas quand en réalité TOUT est dans la grandeur et dans une grandeur qui doit toujours excéder le quotidien, l’accessible et donc, globalement, “l’humain” à l’échelle du spectateur, pour que ça reste un blockbuster qui fait pas trop réfléchir. Ça sa voit aussi dans le fait que tous les personnages oscillent entre deux émotions (toujours EXTRA visibles pour que l’on comprenne bien), à savoir la tristesse sans nuance (crises de pleurs chez tout le monde) ou la joie sans nuance : cf. La fin horriblissime avec girlboss sans nuance Murph qui jette ses feuilles A4 complètement blanches (on dirait Nolan ducoup parce qu’elle a rien écrit elle non plus 😂) sur ses collègues en criant à pleins poumons : “Eurêka” comme si ce film voulait vraiment connaître mes derniers instants avant que je m’étrangle avec le chargeur de mon ordinateur. En bref super film j’ai savouré chaque seconde de détresse absolue qu’il a engendré chez moi et je suis contente d’avoir enfin une raison légitime de refuser catégoriquement le visionnage de L’Odysée.

- 70mm print at TIFF lightbox - I'm really surprised at how much I hated this, the woman intro-ing the movie said that the Nolan brothers massively rewrote the script after picking up the project from Spielberg and it shows. The script is messy, moments of compelling, emotional narrative are occasionally allowed to breach through the walls of exposition but then those emotions are themselves exposited and reiterated to death. The visuals are beautiful if a little dated and overshadowed by more recent successors, my favourite scene visually was in the beginning when they drove through the cornfield chasing a drone. Speaking of the beginning I found the politics of this world to be increadibly messy and nonsensical while also being incredibly heavy handed and unsubtle, saying a lot without any cohesive thought or meaning behind it. I thought a lot of the performances were quite bad, Chastain and Caine especially, I thought Hathaway and the two children were quite good. Damon's performance was really good, him emerging from cryosleep was a haunting high point for the film but the awful scuffle and monologue he delivers afterwords is a cavernous low and he proceeds to fall apart as a character. I was prepared to give this film 2 stars but the awful, self-ashamed "eureka!" delivered by Chastain in the film's climax singlehandedly tanked that. I am actually appalled that this film has the reputation that it does, I guess I wish I saw what everyone else does in it.

Felt it necessary to rewatch since it’d been a decade. Despite its best efforts to conform to a more transcendent cinematic language, drawing from 2001 and other monuments of modernist cinema, the film is fundamentally incapable of embodying that language because of its ideological hostility to the very nature of art. Where 2001 embraces mystery, ambiguity, and the limits of human understanding, Interstellar cannot help but reduce everything to a problem awaiting calculation. The film reeks of the resurgent scientific arrogance that defined much of the 2010s, the kind embodied by Dawkins and his contemporaries. And Elon Musk now a testament of its logical conclusion. It carries the self-assured belief that scientific reasoning and human computation alone are sufficient to save humanity from the very crises those same forces helped create. Even the film’s apparent concession to the irrational, love, is ultimately folded back into the logic of quantification. And thus, even the very medium used to tell this story becomes a means to a self-defeating end. The older I get, the more deeply I believe that the arts are our greatest means of approaching transcendence. Art is how we encounter the sacred, how we gesture toward truths that words, logic, and reason can only circle. To use cinema in service of an ideology that insists every mystery must ultimately be rendered calculable is to undermine the very essence of the art form itself. A truly evil film.

This film is incredibly overrated. I had high expectations coming into this film; due to all the praise online deeming it a ‘masterpiece’ and one of the ‘greatest movies of all time’,but I was left thoroughly disappointed. The dialogue in this film is awful in many instances, the prime example being  “love transcends space and time” which is an incredibly idiotic line coming from a NASA scientist, and feels incredibly out of place in a sci-fi drama. Another problem with this film is the lack of character development specifically with characters like Amelia Brand and the other crew members, I had no connection or care for any of these characters, which led to many of the scenes that were intended to be hard-hitting and emotional not resonating with me in the way that they should have. I feel that the writing in this film drags this film down heavily and the conclusion to this film made no sense- Cooper spends the whole movie trying to get back to his daughter just for him to leave again within 30 seconds of finally reuniting. However, this film has a some great qualities such as the breathtaking visuals and the incredible score and a few fantastic moments and great performances fromMatthew McConaughey who gives an awe-inspiring performance as Cooper and the actress who played young murph (who is superb in this film). Despite the lousy dialogue and some of the terrible moments in this film, this is still a decent watch but is no where near as great as people are describing it.

I would love this movie if its amateurish script didn't constantly get in the way and ruin the experience. Let's get the good stuff out of the way first. It's ridiculously spectacular, Space Odyssey-levels of visual ecstasy. And score is just legendary. Zimmer cooked up something with galaxy-level emotional power. I just wish the rest of the movie were good enough to back up that experience. Nolan's overexposition has become a meme for the ages of cinematic history. This movie, maybe along with Inception , is the quintessential example of Nolan's problem with having his characters explain information in ways that make the in-world conversations border on the ridiculous and unnatural. And look, it's not as though exposition needs to be avoided altogether, particularly when you're dealing with stories rich in scientific concepts. The more substantive criticism is that Nolan repeatedly relies on redundant exposition: characters explain concepts they could plausibly be expected to already understand so that we can follow along, and important information gets explained over and over. Even worse, the problem plagues the thematic material too. Characters don't merely embody the movie's themes, they frequently state them outright. There's Cooper's whole speech about how we're explorers and how we used to look up at the stars with a sense of wonder, Brand's speech about love being the one thing that transcends dimensions, Mann's speeches about human survival instinct and about connection to our loved ones being our last thought when facing death. And then there's the entire dialogue between TARS and Cooper in the tesseract basically walking us through various revelations that are actually taking place on screen. One particularly hilarious case comes when Dr. Brand tells Cooper how inspiring and extraordinary it is that humanity is reaching for the stars and NASA is sending a team to another galaxy, specifically mentioning Mann as a referent. She then tells him that out there they'll face enormous odds, including death, but not evil, never evil. Guess who turns out to be a villain later on. In general, I wouldn't be too negative about this because, regrettably, I've learned to live with this particular Nolan affliction. I could put up with all the overexposition if underneath it all there were a properly constructed script. But Nolan seems to be actively trying to make sure there isn't one. Buckle up, 'cause I'll name some that especially burn me. Cooper stumbles upon what we are told is the most secret base on Earth, where NASA has spent years preparing a space mission, and within ten minutes he's offered the job of piloting the mission. Put aside the fact that it's apparently perfectly plausible for a father and his daughter to infiltrate the world's most secret installation. NASA just happens to desperately need Cooper at exactly the moment he arrives, and Brand effectively recruits him on the spot. I guess we are meant to just believe that the program, in all of its years of preparation, could not find a single pilot fit for the task. The movie is also terribly selective with the information the characters have and/or choose to use. Consider Miller's planet, which should have been recognized as a dubious candidate much earlier. The enormous time dilation means Miller could only have spent a very short amount of her own time on the surface before the Endurance arrived, as explicitly revealed by Brand later on. This effectively means that the positive signal must have represented very little actual observation. The crew knows this, yet they decide to go anyway. This is made even stupider and more contrived by the fact that they explicitly discuss the enormous time cost of going down to the planet beforehand. Another example is Mann's deception. We are meant to believe that the fabricated data about the planet's habitability, which I presume must include a substantial amount of information, somehow survives whatever scrutiny NASA and the Endurance crew are capable of performing. Bear in mind this is humanity's most important scientific endeavour, the last chance of survival for the entire species, so I would assume some extra care on their part. Similarly, there's Professor Brand's lie about the gravity equation. If Brand has known for years that Plan A is impossible, then a substantial part of NASA's operation becomes futile. They're spending years constructing a space station whose purpose is to evacuate humanity, even though the man running the program already knows they won't get far. Not only are we meant to understand that either NASA's higher-ups know and decide to dedicate resources to nothing, or they don't, but we are also meant to believe that no other scientist researching the problem reaches the same conclusion. Speaking of information management, I find it terribly odd that the future humans who possess the ability to manipulate spacetime, create and place wormholes, and construct the tesseract are unable to communicate the required information to humanity themselves. The explanation is that they require Cooper because they supposedly cannot locate or connect to the appropriate moment themselves. But it's not clear why they couldn't have dealt with this by telling someone else. There is also a ridiculously high degree of accidentality involved in the whole gravity-in-the-watch thing and in everything that has to happen for that chain of events to work. Like, we are meant to believe Murph would just happen to connect the dots and realize it's her father talking to her interdimensionally from the fact that there was this anomaly in her room that she stumbled upon when she was 10. Not only that, but she leaves the watch there for just enough time for Cooper to encode what I imagine is highly complex mathematical information, and then just decides to come back and pick it up. Then there's the whole "love transcends dimensions" bullshit, which isn't a plot hole in itself, just some extremely corny shit that robs the movie of a lot of its gravitas by introducing a cheap thematic device that is philosophically naive and dramatically lazy. The characters aren't doing the script any favors either. Cooper is a fucking terrible father. He gets into an argument with Murph's teachers and the whole thing ends with her getting suspended. He seems almost proud of the confrontation and barely concerned about the fact that his daughter has been kicked out of school. Meanwhile, his relationship with Tom might as well come with a giant sign saying "spare child". For a movie so obsessed with the transcendent power of familial love, Cooper's love is hilariously selective. The ending makes it even worse. After spending the entire movie desperately trying to get back to Murph and his family, Cooper finally reunites with his daughter after she's been brought out of cryosleep specifically to see him, has what feels like a two-minute conversation with her, and then just fucking leaves again. The father-daughter bond that supposedly transcends space and time apparently doesn't extend to sticking around for a slightly longer catch-up. And apparently being a terrible decision-maker is hereditary. Tom stubbornly ignores medical advice while his wife and son are visibly suffering from the dust, seemingly more willing to keep his family in a death trap than listen to what the doctors have to say. Then Murph decides that the reasonable way to get Tom out of the house is to set his crops on fire. You know, the crops of a dying Earth where humanity is facing catastrophic food shortages. On top of all this, I'm a known Matthew McConaughey hater. I despise the nonchalant, couldn't-give-a-shit energy he brings to every single one of his characters, and nothing is different here. I can't stand all the grunting and whispering while gazing around. It's annoying. I would keep tearing this apart, but my friends have recently complained that I abuse them with overly long reviews, so I'll leave the rant at that. (I won't stop doing it.)

The production design is well crafted, colour grading is decent, the space stuff itself seems to have been thoroughly researched, and I can’t deny the score is well composed. Also, I think I just prefer 2002: A Space Odyseey as far as space travel films go, that one got weirder with it decades earlier and leaves further unanswered questions in its wake. Also, the World of Tomorrow shorts emotionally connect with me way more while also balancing a combination of weirdness and absurdity for that matter. I think I know what I’m looking for in Sci Fi at this point, and I don’t think this film is quite it with its attempts to be sentimental and tear jerking. This has its moments, don’t get me wrong, but they’re a bit too spread out for me across the almost three hour runtime for me to get into it fully. A lot of sci-fi movies get so caught up in quantum mechanics and space travel that they feel cold and robotic. Interstellar does the exact opposite.
